label: Lesson 4
title: Interaction of light with matter
summary: When light meets matter it can be reflected, refracted, transmitted, absorbed, scattered or emitted. This lesson surveys each interaction and shows why the matching of photon energy to energy gaps is the key to absorption and emission.

intro.text: Light rarely passes through matter untouched. Depending on the material and the wavelength, it may bounce off, bend, pass straight through, be absorbed, be scattered in all directions, or be given back later as emission. Each of these interactions is a tool in spectroscopy.
This lesson walks through the main types and highlights the principle that runs through them all: a photon is absorbed only when its energy matches a gap between two energy levels in the material.

intro.title: The idea that links them all
intro.body: A photon is absorbed only if its energy matches the exact gap between two levels of the material. Different materials have different gaps, so they interact with different wavelengths of light.

sections.title: Reflection, refraction and transmission
sections.summary: Light can bounce off a surface, bend as it crosses a boundary, or pass straight through a transparent medium.
keyPoints: Reflection is the bouncing of light off a surface such as a mirror or polished metal.
Refraction is the bending of light as it passes between media in which it travels at different speeds.
Transmission is the passing of light straight through a material with little or no disruption.
A material can reflect, refract and transmit at once, in different proportions.

blocks.text: The simplest interactions happen at the surface. *Reflection* sends light back from a surface, as at a mirror or a polished metal. *Refraction* bends light as it crosses from one medium into another, such as from air into water or a glass prism, because the speed of light differs in the two media. The same bending separates white light into its colours.

*Transmission* is the passage of light straight through a material with little disturbance, as through clear glass or clean air. A single window pane shows all three at once: some light reflects off the surface, some refracts as it enters and leaves, and most passes through unchanged.

blocks.title: One pane, three effects
blocks.body: Stand at a lit window at night. You see the room reflected (reflection), distant lights slightly displaced if the glass is thick (refraction), and the outside scene through it (transmission). The same photon can do different things depending only on where it meets the glass.

sections.title: Absorption
sections.summary: A material absorbs a photon only when the photon energy matches the gap between two of its energy levels; the absorbed energy becomes heat or lifts an electron.
keyPoints: Absorption occurs when matter takes the energy of a photon.
A photon is absorbed only if its energy matches the gap to a higher energy level.
The absorbed energy can appear as heat or as an electron promoted to a higher level.
Different materials absorb different wavelengths because their energy levels differ.

blocks.text: *Absorption* is the taking up of a photon’s energy by matter. The energy may be converted to heat or used to lift an electron to a higher energy level. What decides whether absorption happens at all is a match: the photon energy must equal the gap between the electron’s current level and a higher one.

Because atoms and molecules have their own fixed sets of energy levels, each material absorbs its own characteristic wavelengths. A photon whose energy does not bridge any gap passes through unabsorbed. The absorbed energy then reappears, either as heat or as a promoted electron that will later fall back.

This wavelength selectivity explains a familiar medical fact. Soft tissue and dense bone have different atomic structures and different energy gaps, so they absorb X-ray photons to different degrees. High-energy X-rays pass through soft tissue but are blocked by bone, which is exactly why bone shows up on a radiograph.

blocks.alt: An energy-level diagram: on the left a photon lifts an electron to a higher level (absorption), and on the right the electron falls back and emits a photon of the same energy (emission).
blocks.caption: Absorption and emission. A photon of energy ΔE lifts the electron up; when it falls back, a photon of the same energy is emitted. Only certain energies fit the fixed level gaps, so spectra show sharp lines.

blocks.title: The wavelength a molecule absorbs
blocks.given: A molecule has an energy gap of 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ J between two of its levels. What wavelength of light does it absorb? Take h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s.
steps: The absorbed photon must have energy ΔE = hc/λ, so λ = hc/ΔE.
That is 620 nm, in the red part of the visible spectrum.
blocks.result: The molecule absorbs light of about 620 nm, so it takes the red out of white light and looks its complementary colour (blue-green).

blocks.title: Absorption is the heart of spectroscopy
blocks.body: An absorption spectrum is a map of the energy gaps in a material, read by finding which wavelengths are missing from the light that passes through. This single idea underlies UV–visible, infrared, atomic absorption and many other techniques.

sections.title: Scattering
sections.summary: Scattering deflects light in many directions when it meets small particles, and its strength rises steeply as wavelength falls, which is why the sky is blue.
keyPoints: Scattering occurs when light is deflected in many directions by atoms or small particles.
The scattered light leaves in directions other than the original beam.
Scattering by particles much smaller than the wavelength is stronger for shorter wavelengths.
This strong short-wavelength scattering makes the daytime sky blue and sunsets red.

blocks.text: *Scattering* happens when light meets atoms or small particles and is deflected in every direction rather than being absorbed or passing straight through. The light is not destroyed; it is redirected, so it appears to come from the scattering centres as well as from the original source.

For particles much smaller than the wavelength of the light, the strength of scattering rises steeply as the wavelength shortens. Blue light, with its shorter wavelength, is scattered far more strongly than red. That is why looking at the sky away from the Sun you see scattered blue light, while light that comes straight through the atmosphere toward you at sunset has lost much of its blue and looks red.

blocks.alt: Two panels: Rayleigh scattering re-emits light of the same energy and colour in all directions, while Raman scattering shifts the photon energy by an amount set by a molecular vibration.
blocks.caption: Scattering. Rayleigh scattering is elastic: the light keeps its colour. Raman scattering is inelastic: a little energy is exchanged with a vibration, so the scattered light is shifted in colour.

blocks.title: The blue sky and the red sunset
blocks.body: Sunlight enters the atmosphere and is scattered by molecules. Shorter wavelengths scatter more, so blue is spread across the sky. At sunset the light travels a longer path and the blue is scattered away before it reaches you, leaving the red that survives the journey.

blocks.text: Scattering is also used deliberately in spectroscopy. Raman scattering, in which light exchanges a little energy with molecular vibrations, gives a fingerprint of a sample and does not require the light to be absorbed.

sections.title: Emission
sections.summary: Emission is the release of light by matter, whether through heat, chemical reaction, or excited electrons falling back to lower energy levels.
keyPoints: Emission is the release of light by matter.
Incandescence is emission caused by heat; luminescence is emission from chemical or other non-thermal excitation.
Fluorescence is emission when an excited electron drops to a lower energy level and releases a photon.
The emitted photon’s energy matches the gap the electron falls across.

blocks.text: If absorption takes energy in, *emission* gives it back as light. Matter can emit light in several ways. The most familiar is *incandescence*, in which heat alone excites the material until it glows, as in a hot filament or a glowing ember.

When the excitation comes from a chemical reaction rather than heat, the emission is called *luminescence*. Bioluminescence, as in a firefly, is a chemical reaction that releases energy as light. When an excited electron simply drops from a higher level to a lower one and gives off the difference as a photon, the process is *fluorescence* or, more generally, photoluminescence.

items: *Luminescence*: emission driven by a chemical or other non-thermal process.
*Fluorescence*: emission as an excited electron falls to a lower level and releases a photon.

blocks.text: In every case the energy of the emitted photon matches the gap the electron falls across. Emission spectra are therefore the mirror image of absorption spectra: they report the same energy levels, seen from the other direction.

sections.title: The interaction types together
sections.summary: The six main interactions, taken together, describe everything that can happen when light meets matter, and each is the basis of a spectroscopic method.
keyPoints: Light can be reflected, refracted, transmitted, absorbed, scattered or emitted.
Absorption and emission depend on matching photon energy to energy gaps.
Scattering does not require absorption and gives its own information.
Each interaction is the working principle of one or more spectroscopic techniques.

blocks.text: Bring the interactions together and you have a complete account of what can happen when light meets matter.

items: *Refraction*: light bends as it changes medium.
*Transmission*: light passes through with little disruption.
*Absorption*: matter takes in the photon’s energy, if the energy matches a gap.
*Scattering*: light is deflected in many directions by small particles.
*Emission*: matter releases light as energy is given back.

blocks.text: Two of these, absorption and emission, are governed by the matching of photon energy to energy levels and are the foundation of most spectroscopy. Scattering needs no absorption and yields its own information about vibrations and structure. Reflection, refraction and transmission are the passive behaviours that instruments rely on to steer and separate light.

blocks.title: From interactions to techniques
blocks.body: Each interaction is the seed of a technique: absorption gives UV–visible and IR spectroscopy, emission gives fluorescence and flame emission, scattering gives Raman, and refraction gives prism dispersion. Knowing the interaction is knowing the method.

cta.title: Check what you have learned
cta.body: Take the Lesson 4 quiz on reflection, refraction, transmission, absorption, scattering and emission.

questions.question: The bouncing of light off a mirror is called:
questions.explanation: Reflection is light bouncing off a surface. In a mirror it follows the law of reflection, with the angle of incidence equal to the angle of reflection.

questions.question: Light passing straight through clear glass with little disturbance is an example of:
questions.explanation: Transmission is the passage of light through a material with little disruption, as through clear glass or clean air.

questions.question: Light bends as it passes from air into water because:
options: Its speed changes between the media
It is emitted by the water
questions.explanation: Refraction bends light because the speed of light differs in the two media. The change in speed at the boundary turns the wavefront.

questions.question: A photon is absorbed by an atom when:
options: Its energy matches the gap between two energy levels
It is always absorbed regardless of energy
questions.explanation: Absorption requires the photon energy to match the gap between the electron’s current level and a higher one. A photon that fits no gap passes through unabsorbed.

questions.question: The energy of an absorbed photon can be converted into heat.
questions.explanation: Absorbed energy may raise an electron to a higher level or be dissipated as heat. Either way the photon’s energy has been taken up by the material.

questions.question: X-rays pass through soft tissue but are blocked by bone because:
options: Soft tissue and bone absorb X-rays to different degrees
questions.explanation: Different materials have different atomic structures and energy levels, so they absorb X-rays differently. Bone absorbs X-rays more strongly than soft tissue, which is why it shows up on a radiograph.

questions.question: All materials absorb the same wavelengths of light.
questions.explanation: Each material has its own set of energy levels, so it absorbs only the wavelengths whose photon energies match its gaps. Different materials therefore absorb different wavelengths.

questions.question: Scattering of light differs from absorption because:
options: The light is redirected rather than absorbed
The light is emitted as heat
The light changes frequency to zero
questions.explanation: In scattering the light is deflected in new directions rather than absorbed. It is redirected, not destroyed, so it can be observed coming from the scattering particles.

questions.question: The daytime sky is blue mainly because:
options: Short wavelengths are scattered more strongly than long ones
Blue light is emitted by the sky
Blue light is absorbed by air
questions.explanation: Scattering by small molecules rises steeply as wavelength shortens, so blue light is scattered across the sky much more than red light.

questions.question: Which are true of scattering? Select all that apply.
options: Light leaves in directions other than the original beam
It is stronger for shorter wavelengths
It always converts light to heat
questions.explanation: Scattering redirects light, can occur without absorption, and is stronger at shorter wavelengths. It does not simply convert light to heat.

questions.question: The glowing of a hot metal filament is an example of:
questions.explanation: Incandescence is emission caused by heat. A hot filament glows because it is thermally excited.

questions.question: Fluorescence occurs when:
options: An excited electron drops to a lower level and releases a photon
Light passes straight through a material
questions.explanation: Fluorescence is emission as an excited electron falls to a lower energy level, releasing the energy difference as a photon.

questions.question: Emission of light by a firefly is an example of:
questions.explanation: Bioluminescence, as in a firefly, is luminescence: light produced by a chemical reaction rather than by heat.

questions.question: Emission spectra reveal the same energy levels as absorption spectra.
questions.explanation: Emission and absorption both involve the same energy gaps, seen from opposite directions. An emission line marks a downward jump that an absorption line would mark as an upward one.

questions.question: Which of these are ways light can interact with matter? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Light can be absorbed, emitted or scattered (as well as reflected, refracted and transmitted). Voltage is an electrical quantity, not an interaction of light with matter.

questions.question: When light passes from air into glass at an angle, it bends:
questions.explanation: On entering the denser medium the light slows, which bends it towards the normal. Leaving a denser medium for a less dense one bends it away from the normal instead.

questions.question: A substance looks green in white light because it:
options: emits green light of its own
absorbs most colours but reflects or transmits green
questions.explanation: An object has the colour of the light it sends to your eye. A green object reflects or transmits green and absorbs the other colours. (A glowing object is different: it emits its own light.)

questions.question: Rayleigh scattering is stronger for shorter wavelengths, which is one reason the sky looks blue.
questions.explanation: Air molecules scatter short wavelengths far more than long ones, roughly as 1/λ⁴. Blue light from the Sun is scattered across the sky, so we see blue coming from all directions.

questions.question: Light is emitted from an atom when:
options: an electron drops from a higher to a lower energy level
an electron is added to the atom
questions.explanation: An electron that has been raised to a higher level can fall back down. The lost energy leaves as a photon whose energy equals the gap between the levels.

questions.question: A molecule absorbs a photon of energy 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Find the wavelength absorbed, in nanometres. Take hc = 1.99 × 10⁻²⁵ J m.
questions.explanation: λ = hc / ΔE = 1.99 × 10⁻²⁵ / 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 4.98 × 10⁻⁷ m = 498 nm, which is blue-green light.

questions.question: Which of these can happen when light meets matter? Select all that apply.
options: light always passes through completely unchanged
questions.explanation: Light can be reflected, absorbed or scattered, and often a mixture of all three. It is not true that light always passes through unchanged: that is the special case of a fully transparent, non-absorbing material.

questions.question: When light meets matter, it may be:
questions.explanation: An incoming beam can be split into a reflected part, an absorbed part, a transmitted part and a scattered part. The balance depends on the material and the wavelength.

questions.question: Specular reflection is reflection from:
options: a smooth surface, giving a clear image
a rough surface, giving no image
questions.explanation: A smooth surface reflects a parallel beam as a parallel beam, preserving the image; a rough surface scatters it.

questions.question: Diffuse reflection occurs because:
options: a rough surface sends light in many directions
the surface absorbs all the light
questions.explanation: Roughness makes different patches reflect in different directions, so the light is spread out rather than forming a mirror image.

questions.question: A material looks transparent when it:
options: transmits most incident light without much absorption
questions.explanation: Transparency means light passes through with little absorption or scattering, over the range of wavelengths concerned.

questions.question: The colour of an opaque object is set by:
questions.explanation: An opaque object shows the colours it reflects strongly; the rest are absorbed. A red object reflects red and absorbs the other colours.

questions.question: A black surface absorbs most of the light that falls on it.
questions.explanation: Black means little light is reflected; almost all of the incident light is absorbed.

questions.question: Refraction happens because light changes speed when it crosses between media.
questions.explanation: The change of speed across the boundary bends the wavefront, which is what refraction is.

questions.question: A white surface reflects most of the visible wavelengths.
questions.explanation: A white surface reflects all visible colours about equally, so it looks white under white light.

questions.question: What can happen to light when it meets matter? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Light can be reflected, absorbed or transmitted, and it can also be scattered. It is not turned into a gravitational wave.

questions.question: A surface reflects 30% of the incident light and absorbs none. What fraction of the light is transmitted?
questions.explanation: Reflection takes 30%, so 70% is transmitted: 0.70.

questions.question: A sample absorbs 60% of the light passing through it. What percentage is transmitted?
questions.explanation: Whatever is not absorbed is transmitted, so 100 − 60 = 40%.

questions.question: A molecule absorbs a photon when:
options: the photon energy matches the gap between two of its energy levels
questions.explanation: Absorption is resonant: it happens when the photon energy equals the spacing between an occupied and a higher level.

questions.question: An absorption spectrum appears as:
options: dark lines on a bright continuous background
bright lines on a dark background
questions.explanation: A sample removes the wavelengths it absorbs from a continuous beam, leaving dark lines against the bright background.

questions.question: In the Beer–Lambert law A = εcl, the absorbance is proportional to:
options: the concentration and the path length
questions.explanation: Absorbance rises with concentration c and path length l, with the molar absorptivity ε setting the response at that wavelength.

questions.question: A solution that absorbs green light strongly will look:
options: magenta or reddish-purple, the complementary colour
questions.explanation: The transmitted light is what remains after green is removed, giving the complementary colour, which is magenta for green.

questions.question: Absorbing a photon raises a molecule to a higher energy level.
questions.explanation: The energy of the photon is taken up as internal energy, promoting the molecule from a lower to a higher level.

questions.question: A sample absorbs the same fraction of light at every wavelength.
questions.explanation: Absorption is wavelength-dependent. A substance absorbs strongly at its characteristic wavelengths and weakly elsewhere.

questions.question: The absorbance in the Beer–Lambert law depends on which of the following? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Absorbance is A = εcl. The container colour does not enter the law.

questions.question: A solution has molar absorptivity ε = 500 L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹, concentration 0.020 mol/L and path length 1.0 cm. Find the absorbance.
A solution of concentration 0.10 mol/L in a 2.0 cm cell has an absorbance of 1.0. Find its molar absorptivity in L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹.
Scattering is best described as:
options: the redirection of light by particles or molecules
questions.explanation: In scattering, light is redirected in many directions by molecules or particles, without necessarily being absorbed.

questions.question: The intensity of Rayleigh scattering is proportional to:
questions.explanation: Rayleigh scattering falls off steeply with wavelength as 1/λ⁴, so short wavelengths scatter far more strongly.

questions.question: The sky looks blue mainly because:
options: short wavelengths are scattered more strongly by air molecules
questions.explanation: By the 1/λ⁴ rule, blue light is scattered much more than red, so blue reaches our eyes from all directions.

questions.question: A sunset looks red because:
options: blue light is scattered away, leaving the longer wavelengths
red light is scattered more strongly
the Sun cools in the evening
questions.explanation: Near the horizon, light travels a long path through the air, so much of the blue is scattered out and red dominates.

questions.question: Raman scattering involves:
options: a change in the photon energy because of molecular vibrations
absorption followed by re-emission at the same energy
questions.explanation: In Raman scattering a small amount of energy is exchanged with molecular vibrations, so the scattered photon has a slightly different energy.

questions.question: Rayleigh scattering is elastic, so the scattered photon has the same energy as the incident one.
questions.explanation: Elastic means no energy is transferred, so the photon keeps its energy and only its direction changes.

questions.question: Raman scattering changes the energy of the scattered photon.
questions.explanation: The photon gives up or gains a quantum of vibrational energy, so its energy shifts. This shift identifies the molecule.

questions.question: Shorter wavelengths are scattered more strongly than longer ones.
questions.explanation: The 1/λ⁴ dependence means blue light scatters much more than red, which is why the sky is blue and sunsets are red.

questions.question: Which are true of Rayleigh scattering? Select all that apply.
options: it explains the blue of the sky
questions.explanation: Rayleigh scattering is elastic, follows a 1/λ⁴ law and colours the sky. It does not change the photon energy; that is Raman scattering.

questions.question: Rayleigh intensity varies as 1/λ⁴. If the wavelength is doubled, by what factor does the intensity change? Give the factor (for example 0.25).
questions.explanation: Doubling λ multiplies intensity by 1/2⁴ = 1/16 = 0.0625.

questions.question: If the wavelength is halved, by what factor does the Rayleigh scattering intensity increase?
questions.explanation: Intensity ∝ 1/λ⁴. Halving λ gives a factor of 2⁴ = 16.

questions.question: Light is emitted when:
options: an excited atom or molecule drops to a lower energy level
questions.explanation: Emission follows a downward transition: the energy released appears as a photon.

questions.question: An emission spectrum appears as:
options: bright lines on a dark background
dark lines on a bright background
questions.explanation: A hot gas of isolated atoms emits at its characteristic wavelengths only, giving bright lines against darkness.

questions.question: Fluorescence differs from phosphorescence mainly in:
questions.explanation: Fluorescence is prompt; phosphorescence lingers because the excited state is long-lived. Colour, intensity and polarisation are not the defining difference.

questions.question: The energy of an emitted photon equals:
options: the energy difference between the two levels involved
the energy of any absorbed photon
the kinetic energy of the atom
questions.explanation: The photon carries away exactly the energy lost by the atom in dropping between the two levels.

questions.question: A line spectrum is evidence that:
options: the energy levels in atoms are discrete
questions.explanation: Sharp lines come only from transitions between discrete levels, so a line spectrum reveals quantised energy.

questions.question: An atom can emit a photon only when it moves from a higher to a lower energy level.
questions.explanation: Emission requires a downward transition. Going up requires absorption of energy instead.

questions.question: A hot gas of isolated atoms produces a continuous emission spectrum.
questions.explanation: Isolated atoms give a line spectrum at their characteristic wavelengths. A continuous spectrum comes from a hot dense body.

questions.question: The wavelengths in an emission spectrum match those missing from the corresponding absorption spectrum.
questions.explanation: Both come from the same set of level spacings, so the lines appear at the same wavelengths, bright in emission and dark in absorption.

questions.question: Which are true of emission? Select all that apply.
options: the photon energy equals the level gap
it gives bright lines for isolated atoms
it always requires a photon to be absorbed first
questions.explanation: Emission follows a downward transition and reveals the level gap as a bright line. Excitation need not be by light; it can be by heat or a discharge.

questions.question: An electron falls from an energy of −3.4 eV to −13.6 eV. Find the energy of the emitted photon in electronvolts.
questions.explanation: The energy released is the gap: −3.4 − (−13.6) = 10.2 eV.

questions.question: Find the wavelength, in nanometres, of a photon of energy 2.0 eV. Use hc = 1240 eV·nm.
Which interaction reveals the energy levels of a molecule?
options: absorption of light at specific wavelengths
questions.explanation: A molecule absorbs only photons matching its level gaps, so its absorption pattern maps out those gaps.

questions.question: Which process gives information about molecular vibrations through a shift in photon energy?
questions.explanation: The Raman shift is the energy exchanged with a molecular vibration, so the shift reports on the vibrations.

questions.question: A gas that emits a line spectrum must have:
questions.explanation: Sharp emission lines come from transitions between discrete levels; without them the lines could not be sharp.

questions.question: Taken together, reflection, refraction, absorption, scattering and emission:
options: describe how light interacts with matter
questions.explanation: These are the ways light and matter exchange and redirect energy, and together they form the basis of spectroscopy.

questions.question: Which interaction is used in optical spectroscopy to identify a substance?
questions.explanation: Each substance has a fingerprint of absorbed wavelengths, so measuring absorption identifies it.

questions.question: Different substances absorb light at different characteristic wavelengths.
questions.explanation: The pattern of absorbed wavelengths is unique to each substance, much like a fingerprint.

questions.question: The absorption and emission spectra of a given substance are related.
questions.explanation: Both arise from the same set of energy-level spacings, so the lines occur at matching wavelengths.

questions.question: Scattering always leaves the photon energy unchanged.
questions.explanation: Rayleigh scattering is elastic and leaves the energy unchanged, but Raman scattering shifts the photon energy by a vibrational quantum.

questions.question: Which can be used to identify a substance? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The absorption, emission and Raman spectra are all characteristic fingerprints. Mass by itself does not identify a substance.

questions.question: Which interactions involve a transfer of energy to the matter? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Absorption and Raman scattering put energy into the matter, and emission takes it out. Specular reflection is elastic and transfers none.

questions.question: A beam of 100 units is reflected (20), absorbed (30) and scattered (10). How much is transmitted?
questions.explanation: By conservation, the transmitted amount is 100 − 20 − 30 − 10 = 40 units.

questions.question: A sample transmits 25% of the incident light. Find its absorbance, A = −log₁₀(T), with T = 0.25.
